title: DenseSteer: Steering Small Language Models towards Dense Math Reasoning
claim: Stronger models solve problems with fewer reasoning steps and higher per-step information density, a trend that motivates dense reasoning.
layout: 2 vertically stacked scatter plots, shared legend on top, dashed trend lines
description: Two vertically stacked scatter plots share a legend at the top. The legend lists six Qwen2.5-Instruct models (1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B, 72B), each with its own colored marker. In both plots the y-axis is Accuracy, from about 35 to 100, and each point has small horizontal error bars. The top plot puts average number of reasoning steps (6.5 to 8.0) on the x-axis. A dashed line slopes downward. The strong models cluster at upper left, with about 6.5 steps and 90–95% accuracy. The 3B model sits at about 7.7 steps and 83%. The 1.5B model sits at the bottom right, at about 7.9 steps and 37%. The bottom plot puts average reasoning density ρ (tokens per step, 36 to 40) on the x-axis. Its dashed trend line slopes upward. The 1.5B model is at the lower left, the 3B model is in the middle, and the 72B model is at the upper right. The eye goes first to the dashed trend lines and the isolated 1.5B outlier.
caption: Analysis of Reasoning Patterns on GSM8K. For each model and each GSM8K test problem, we sample 8 responses. Error bars denote $\pm 1$ standard error of the mean (SEM), computed over question-level averages. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct models, stronger models often use fewer reasoning steps and higher per-step density than smaller, lower-accuracy models. This coarse trend motivates our focus on dense, model-aligned reasoning.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning abilities, while smaller models (<= 3B parameters) significantly underperform on multi-step reasoning tasks. Based on empirical analyses of the Qwen-2.5 model family on math reasoning benchmarks, we find that more proficient reasoning is associated with fewer reasoning steps but higher information density per step, a property we term Dense Reasoning. Motivated by this observation, we propose DenseSteer, a training-free inference-time steering framework that enhances small-model reasoning by modulating internal representations toward dense reasoning patterns. Experiments show that our method yields consistent accuracy improvements without increasing token-level Negative Log-Likelihood, highlighting dense reasoning as an effective structural approach to mathematical problem solving.
